nameStory: The name 'Wormseed Sandmat' comes from the plant's tiny, worm-like seeds that have distinctive ridged patterns resembling segmented worms. The 'sandmat' part refers to its growth habit of forming low, sprawling mats in sandy soils, creating a carpet-like appearance close to the ground.
description: Wormseed Sandmat is a small, spreading annual plant that hugs the ground like a green carpet. This tiny spurge rarely grows taller than your thumb, instead creeping outward to form circular mats up to a foot across. Its stems are thin and reddish, branching repeatedly to create a dense network of tiny oval leaves that feel smooth and somewhat succulent to the touch.

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: The seeds are the star feature - tiny, ridged, and distinctly worm-like with deep grooves running lengthwise, giving them a segmented appearance like earthworms

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms perfectly circular or nearly circular mats that spread outward from the center, staying completely flat against the ground like a living doily

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Tiny oval leaves about the size of your pinky nail, smooth-edged and slightly thick feeling, arranged oppositely on reddish stems that feel somewhat succulent when pinched

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Microscopic flowers clustered in leaf joints - you'll need a hand lens to see them clearly, appearing as tiny white or pinkish dots

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Thin, often reddish or pinkish stems that branch repeatedly and lie completely flat, exuding a milky sap when broken (like all spurges)

habitat: Look for Wormseed Sandmat in disturbed sandy areas, vacant lots, sidewalk cracks, and along roadsides where the soil is well-drained and often poor. It particularly loves sunny spots with sandy or gravelly soil where few other plants can compete. You'll often find it growing alongside other weedy spurges in urban and suburban settings throughout New England's warmer areas.

seasonality.spring: Seeds germinate in late spring when soil warms up, starting as tiny rosettes that begin spreading outward.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season when the characteristic circular mats become most obvious, with continuous tiny flowering and seed production through the heat.
seasonality.fall: Plants continue growing and producing the distinctive ridged seeds until first frost kills the annual plants.
seasonality.winter: Plants are completely gone, but seeds remain in the soil to germinate next spring.

funFact: Wormseed Sandmat can complete its entire life cycle - from seed to flowering to new seeds - in just 6-8 weeks, allowing it to squeeze in multiple generations per growing season and rapidly colonize disturbed ground.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other small sandmat spurges, especially Prostrate Sandmat and Thymeleaf Sandmat. The key difference is in the seeds - Wormseed Sandmat's seeds look distinctly worm-like with deep ridges, while the others have different surface patterns. Memory trick: 'Wormseed = worm-like ridges.'
contextualKnowledge: Like all spurges, this plant contains a milky latex sap that can cause skin irritation in sensitive people, so avoid getting the sap in your eyes or on cuts. The common name 'sandmat' is used for several low-growing Euphorbia species, so always check the specific scientific name when looking up information.
compareHints: Among New England's sandmat spurges, Wormseed Sandmat is distinguished by its perfectly circular growth pattern and distinctively ridged seeds. Seaside Sandmat grows in coastal dunes and has more linear leaves, while Prostrate Sandmat has rounder seeds without the deep worm-like ridges. Thymeleaf Sandmat has smaller, more crowded leaves and different seed sculpturing.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike other spurges in New England that typically have broader, more conventional leaves, cypress spurge is instantly recognizable by its needle-like foliage.
Among New England's spurges, spotted spurge is unique for its ground-hugging mat formation and distinctly spotted leaves.
Among New England's spurges, seaside sandmat is unique in its completely prostrate, mat-forming habit and coastal habitat.
Among New England spurges, slender leafy spurge is distinguished by its tall, narrow growth form and lance-shaped leaves.
Among New England's spurges, nodding spurge is distinguished by its prostrate, mat-forming growth and drooping flower clusters.
Unlike other New England spurges which are mostly weedy annuals with thin leaves, Donkey Tail is a perennial succulent with thick, fleshy foliage.
Among New England spurges, caper spurge is unique for its large size and architectural growth habit - most other spurges are low-growing weeds or small garden plants.
Unlike the tall, weedy leafy spurge or the ground-hugging spotted spurge, cushion spurge maintains a perfectly rounded, compact form.
Among New England spurges, petty spurge is one of the smallest and most delicate-looking species.
Flowering spurge towers over most of its spurge relatives in New England, which tend to be low, mat-forming plants like spotted spurge or cypress spurge.
Snow-on-the-mountain is easily distinguished from other New England spurges by its distinctive white-margined leaves - most other spurges in our region have plain green foliage.

Leafy spurge stands out from other New England spurges by its tall, upright growth and dense leafy appearance - most of its relatives like spotted spurge and prostrate sandmat are low, sprawling plants.
Among New England spurges, graceful spurge stands out for its relatively tall, upright growth compared to the ground-hugging spotted spurge or prostrate sandmat.
Among New England's spurges, thymeleaf sandmat is distinguished by its ground-hugging mat formation and tiny thyme-like leaves.
Sweet spurge stands out from other New England spurges by its clumping perennial growth habit and relatively large, oval leaves.
Among New England spurges, green poinsettia stands out for its distinctly hairy, toothed leaves - most other spurges have smooth or nearly smooth leaves.
Unlike the needle-like leaves of cypress spurge or the spotted stems of spotted spurge, David's spurge has broader, toothed leaves arranged in opposite pairs.
Unlike other New England spurges that have broader, more typical-looking leaves, grassleaf spurge's ultra-narrow foliage makes it unique in the region.
Among New England's spurges, prostrate sandmat is uniquely flat-growing - most other spurges like cypress spurge or flowering spurge grow upright.
Unlike cypress spurge with its needle-like leaves or spotted spurge that grows as a low mat, eggleaf spurge stands upright with distinctly oval, toothed leaves.
Compared to other New England spurges, Florida hammock sandmat is distinguished by its exceptionally small size and extremely low, tight mat-forming habit.
Matted sandmat is flatter and more perfectly mat-forming than most other spurges in our region.
Among New England's spurges, ribseed sandmat is distinguished by its extremely rare occurrence and the ribbed seeds that give it its name.
